The out-of-service internal inspection interval in one answer

API 653 sets the first out-of-service internal inspection at no more than 10 years after a tank enters service, then lets the owner add cumulative credits for safeguards such as a product-side lining, soil-side cathodic protection, a release prevention barrier (RPB), a qualifying stainless bottom or extra original bottom thickness. The initial interval cannot exceed 20 years without an RPB or 30 years with one. After that first inspection, the next interval comes from the measured bottom corrosion rate and the minimum remaining thickness, under the same 20-year and 30-year caps, or from an owner-commissioned risk-based assessment. Jurisdictional rules override all of it where they are stricter.

The sections above walk through the clause mechanics. This section adds what the clause text leaves to the people running the programme: the factors API 653 says can shorten or lengthen an interval, the evidence an authorized inspector expects before accepting a credit, worked scenarios for common tank configurations, the in-service alternative for bottom-only assessment, the NDE that actually produces the bottom data, and the regulatory overlays in the United States and Canada. Clause references are to the Fifth Edition. Addendum 4 (July 2025) revised the text of the initial-interval clause and the requirements for tank-bottom plate thickness measurement, so confirm every number against the edition and addendum your programme is written to before relying on it.

What API 653 says can shorten or lengthen the interval

Section 6.2 opens the inspection-frequency discussion with a list of considerations rather than a single number. Several factors determine how often a tank should be inspected, and the standard expects the owner and the authorized inspector to weigh them for each tank rather than copy one interval across a tank farm. The 10-year baseline and the Table 6.1 credits are ceilings that apply only when those considerations do not point to something shorter.

The factors fall into five practical groups:

  • The product and how it attacks steel. The nature of the product stored, its temperature, water and sediment content, and whether it contains corrosive species all change the product-side rate. Crude with settled water and sulfate-reducing bacteria behaves very differently from a dry finished product. A change of service, for example converting a gasoline tank to biodiesel or to a heated product, resets the assumptions behind the previous interval.
  • Corrosion rates and allowances. Measured rates from previous inspections, the remaining corrosion allowance and the reliability of the data behind those numbers are the strongest single input. A tank whose last inspection found isolated deep pitting cannot carry forward an interval that assumed uniform thinning.
  • Corrosion prevention systems. Linings, coatings and cathodic protection only earn their value if they are installed to the relevant recommended practice and kept in service. A lining past its expected life or a CP system with lapsed survey records no longer supports a long interval.
  • Consequence and detection. The location of the tank, including its proximity to water, groundwater sensitivity, populated areas and secondary containment, sits alongside leak detection capability and the presence of a double bottom or RPB. A tank that would release into a waterway if the bottom failed warrants a shorter, more conservative cycle than an identical tank inside an impermeable dike with leak detection.
  • Operation and regulation. Changes in operating mode, such as frequent fill and draw cycling, heated service or a move from storage to rapid transfer duty, can accelerate bottom and shell damage. Jurisdictional requirements are listed explicitly; where a regulator prescribes a shorter interval, it governs.

The practical consequence is that the interval on an inspection report should carry its reasoning: the baseline, each credit claimed, the factors considered and any reason the inspector chose something shorter than the maximum. An interval written as a bare date is hard to defend at audit and impossible to re-evaluate when service conditions change.

Evidence an authorized inspector expects before accepting a Table 6.1 credit

Credits are where most extended initial intervals fail review. Table 6.1 does not award time for the existence of a safeguard; it awards time for a safeguard installed and maintained to a named recommended practice. The authorized inspector setting the interval needs records, not assurances. The typical evidence for each credit looks like this:

Safeguard claimedReference practice named by API 653Records an inspector will typically ask forCommon reason the credit is refused
Product-side bottom lining (reinforced or unreinforced)API RP 652Lining specification, surface preparation records, coating inspection and holiday test results, applicator documentation, date appliedNo installation records; lining applied over unknown surface condition; lining type cannot be confirmed as reinforced
Soil-side cathodic protectionAPI RP 651CP design, commissioning survey, periodic survey results showing protection criteria met, rectifier recordsSystem installed but surveys missing or showing inadequate protection; CP added years after service start without baseline data
Release prevention barrierAPI 650 Annex IDesign drawings of the double bottom or liner, leak detection arrangement, construction recordsBarrier exists but leak detection path is blocked or undocumented; barrier not designed to the referenced annex
Stainless steel bottomAPI 650 annexes referenced in Table 6.1Material certificates, fabrication records confirming the annex requirementsMaterial or construction records unavailable
Bottom thicker than the base valueTable 6.1 thickness creditOriginal mill or construction records showing as-built bottom thicknessAs-built thickness unknown, so the credit cannot be calculated

Two points catch owners out repeatedly. First, the credits are tied to the condition that makes them valid: a CP credit implies the system has protected the bottom since service began, so a system added late or left unsurveyed for years undermines the basis. Second, missing construction records are common on older tanks and acquisitions. Where the as-built bottom thickness or lining history cannot be shown, the conservative course is to take the 10-year baseline, inspect, and let measured data drive the subsequent interval.

Worked scenarios for common tank configurations

The scenarios below apply the Fifth Edition credit values described earlier on this page. They are illustrations of the arithmetic, not interval recommendations; the interval for a real tank is set by the owner and the authorized inspector after considering every factor in Section 6.2 and the edition and addendum in force.

Scenario 1: bare carbon steel bottom, no CP, no lining, no RPB, base bottom thickness. No credits apply. The initial internal inspection falls due at no more than 10 years after the tank entered service. This is the default many older terminal tanks sit on, and it is also the right answer whenever credit evidence is missing.

Scenario 2: carbon steel bottom with soil-side CP per API RP 651 and a thin-film product-side lining per API RP 652, no RPB. The arithmetic gives 10 plus 5 for CP plus 2 for the unreinforced lining, or 17 years. That is below the 20-year cap that applies without an RPB, so the arithmetic result stands as the maximum, subject to the Section 6.2 factors.

Scenario 3: same as scenario 2 but with a reinforced thick-film lining and a bottom 3/8 in. thick. The lining now earns 5 rather than 2, giving 10 plus 5 plus 5, or 20, before the thickness credit. The thickness credit adds the excess over 0.25 in. divided by the default rate of 15 mils per year: 0.125 in. divided by 0.015 in. per year is roughly 8.3 years. The sum exceeds 28 years, but without an RPB the initial interval is capped at 20. The extra credits do not carry forward; they simply show that the cap, not the calculation, is governing.

Scenario 4: new tank with an RPB per API 650 Annex I, CP and a reinforced lining. 10 plus 10 plus 5 plus 5 gives 30 years, which meets the 30-year cap that applies with an RPB. Any thickness credit would be absorbed by the cap.

The lesson from scenarios 3 and 4 is that the RPB is what moves the ceiling. Owners planning new construction or a bottom replacement who want a long first cycle should weigh the barrier design at that stage, because it is the only safeguard that raises the cap rather than adding time beneath it.

The in-service alternative when only the bottom needs assessment

API 653 recognises that taking a tank out of service, cleaning it and gas-freeing it is costly and carries its own risk. Where the purpose of the internal inspection is solely to determine the condition and integrity of the tank bottom, the Fifth Edition permits the assessment to be carried out with the tank in service using on-stream methods. These include robotic ultrasonic thickness measurement and other in-service inspection techniques, which may be supplemented by electromagnetic methods, provided the data gathered are sufficient for the authorized inspector to establish the next interval.

The conditions matter more than the permission. The data must be good enough to set an interval, which means adequate coverage of the bottom, including the critical zone near the shell, and enough confidence in measured remaining thickness and corrosion rate. In practice, in-service robotic surveys work best where the product is compatible with the crawler, visibility or coupling conditions are acceptable, and sludge or debris will not mask large areas of plate. They do not inspect the shell interior, roof structure, internal piping or welds in the way an out-of-service visual can, so they answer the bottom question only. Where an in-service survey leaves gaps or ambiguous indications, the authorized inspector may still require an out-of-service inspection.

NDE methods that produce the bottom data, and their limits

The interval is only as good as the bottom data behind it. An out-of-service internal inspection normally combines a screening method for full-floor coverage with a quantitative method for sizing. The table below summarises what each method contributes.

MethodWhat it findsLimits to plan around
Magnetic flux leakage (MFL) floor scanningRapid screening of plate for topside and soil-side metal loss across most of the floorScreening tool; indications need sizing by UT; reduced sensitivity near shell, lap welds and obstructions; thick coatings and plate thickness affect detection
Ultrasonic thickness (UT) prove-upRemaining thickness at MFL indications and at grid or critical-zone locationsPoint measurements; coverage depends on the plan; soil-side pitting can be missed between points
UT corrosion mapping or phased arrayArea thickness maps for annular plates, critical zone and suspect regionsSlower than screening; surface condition and access affect results
Visual examinationPitting, coating failure, weld condition, settlement distortion, internal component damageNeeds cleaned surfaces and adequate lighting; cannot see soil-side loss
Vacuum box testingThrough-wall leaks in bottom welds and repairsLeak test only, not a thickness measurement
Magnetic particle or liquid penetrantSurface cracking at welds, especially shell-to-bottom and near settlement breakover areasSurface methods; need preparation

Two programme decisions follow. Coverage drives confidence: a floor scanned edge to edge with MFL and proven up with UT produces a corrosion rate an inspector can stand behind, while a handful of spot readings does not. If the owner later wants to use a risk-based route for the subsequent interval, the Fifth Edition does not allow corrosion rates from low-effectiveness inspection such as spot UT to be used, so the coverage choice at this inspection shapes the options at the next one. Second, Addendum 4 revised the tank-bottom thickness measurement requirements and points to API RP 575; confirm the measurement approach in your inspection plan against the current addendum before the tank is opened.

Regulatory overlays in the United States and Canada

API 653 is a consensus standard. It becomes mandatory through regulation, contract or the owner's own programme, and several regulators adopt it with their own conditions.

  • PHMSA breakout tanks. 49 CFR 195.432 requires operators to inspect in-service atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks in accordance with API 653, but excludes the standard's risk-based alternative internal inspection interval provision. A regulated breakout tank therefore relies on the corrosion-rate route for subsequent intervals.
  • EPA SPCC. 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) requires bulk storage containers to be tested or inspected for integrity on a regular schedule according to industry standards, combining visual inspection with another technique. API 653 is the usual standard for field-erected tanks; STI SP001 is often used for shop-built tanks. The SPCC plan, certified by a Professional Engineer where required, should state which standard and interval apply to each container.
  • OSHA PSM. Where tanks fall inside a covered process, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires inspection and testing that follows recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, at a frequency consistent with those practices and with prior operating experience. API 653 is commonly cited as that practice for atmospheric tanks.
  • States and local authorities. State environmental agencies, fire marshals and local codes can impose their own tank inspection or leak detection requirements. Confirm with the authority having jurisdiction.
  • Canada. Requirements are provincial and territorial, typically through fire codes and environmental regulation of storage tank systems, and federally regulated sites have their own rules. Many Canadian owners use API 653 as the inspection basis; confirm the applicable provincial regulation and any prescribed frequency with the regulator.

Common mistakes that shorten intervals or fail audits

  • Claiming credits without records. A lining or CP credit with no installation or survey evidence will not survive review, and an interval built on it becomes non-compliant retroactively.
  • Applying a fleet interval. Copying one interval across tanks in different services ignores Section 6.2 and is a common audit finding.
  • Treating the cap as the target. 20 and 30 years are maximums. The calculated interval or the inspector's judgement often governs at a shorter date.
  • Thin data at the first inspection. Limited floor coverage produces an uncertain corrosion rate, which forces a shorter subsequent interval and can rule out other routes later.
  • Ignoring service changes. A new product, heating or higher cycling invalidates the assumptions behind the existing interval until it is re-evaluated.
  • Using an outdated edition. Programmes written to an earlier edition or addendum may cite clause numbers and text that have since changed.

More questions on the API 653 internal inspection interval

What does API Std 653 require for out-of-service internal inspection intervals on aboveground welded steel storage tanks?

A first internal inspection no later than 10 years after service begins, extendable by cumulative safeguard credits up to 20 years without an RPB or 30 years with one. Subsequent intervals come from measured bottom corrosion rates and minimum remaining thickness under the same caps, or from an owner-commissioned risk-based assessment where the jurisdiction permits it.

What factors shorten the API 653 internal inspection interval?

Aggressive product or contaminants, high measured corrosion rates, unreliable or limited inspection data, failed or undocumented linings and CP, sensitive locations, weak leak detection, increased fill cycling or heated service, a change of service, and jurisdictional rules that prescribe shorter intervals.

Does a release prevention barrier extend the interval?

Yes. In the Fifth Edition an RPB per API 650 Annex I earns a 10-year credit and raises the cap from 20 to 30 years, for both the initial and subsequent intervals.

Can a tank bottom be inspected without taking the tank out of service?

Where the internal inspection is solely to assess the bottom, API 653 permits in-service methods such as robotic ultrasonic thickness measurement, which may be supplemented by electromagnetic methods, if the data are sufficient to set the next interval.

Can PHMSA-regulated breakout tanks use risk-based intervals?

No. 49 CFR 195.432 adopts API 653 for breakout tanks but excludes its risk-based alternative internal inspection interval provision.

Who sets the internal inspection interval?

The owner/operator with its API 653 authorized inspector, within the code and any jurisdictional requirement. NDE contractors provide the data but do not set the interval.

Does the first inspection establish the corrosion rate?

It establishes the first measured bottom rate, which then drives the subsequent interval through the minimum remaining thickness calculation. Better coverage gives a more defensible rate.

What changed in API 653 Addendum 4?

Addendum 4, published July 2025, revised the initial internal interval clause and the requirements for tank-bottom plate thickness measurement, with reference to API RP 575. Check the full addendum before updating inspection plans.
